## Background

### Study Area and Site Selection

The analysis covers Colorado USGS streamgages from the GAGES-II dataset (both reference and non-reference). Site metadata --- including drainage area, basin elevation and slope, upstream dam storage, and GAGES-II classification --- were assembled from the GAGES-II attribute tables (`conterm_basinid.txt`, `conterm_topo.txt`, `conterm_hydromod_dams.txt`, `conterm_bas_classif.txt`). Sites were flagged as regulated if upstream normal storage exceeded 1,000 acre-feet (1.233 mcm), following the threshold used by Davenport et al. (2020). Of the 206 Colorado sites in the dataset, 63 are unregulated and 143 are regulated by this criterion.

### Streamflow Peak Extraction

Daily maximum discharge was derived from USGS unit (15-minute) data. Peaks over threshold (POT) were identified using a per-site threshold equal to the median daily maximum flow (the 50th percentile of the daily maximum flow record), which also serves as the GPD location parameter $\mu$ in downstream frequency fitting following Yu et al. (2022). Peaks were declustered using the minimum time-separation criterion from Livneh et al. (2024): $\theta = 5 + \ln(1.6092 \cdot A)$ days, where $A$ is drainage area in km². The output (`pot_peaks_all.rds`) is one row per site-day within each peak window. The dataset contains approximately 21,211 distinct peaks across all 206 sites.

### WLDAS Climate Variable Extraction

Hydrometeorological drivers were obtained from the Western Land Data Assimilation System (WLDAS), a Noah-MP land surface model product at 0.01° spatial resolution covering CONUS. Daily NetCDF files were processed in parallel using `exactextractr`, extracting basin-mean values for rainfall flux (`rainf_flux`), snowfall flux (`snowf_flux`), and snowmelt flux (`qsm_flux`), as well as basin maximum, standard deviation, coefficient of variation, and wetted fraction (fraction of cells exceeding 1 mm/day) for those three variables. All flux variables were converted from kg m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ to mm/day. WLDAS spatial extent and CRS were set from known grid parameters (3591 $\times$ 2787 cells, 0.01° resolution, CONUS extent) rather than from file metadata, which returns pixel rather than geographic coordinates. Outputs were written as date-partitioned Parquet files.

### Flood Type Classification

Three classification schemes are implemented. The Davenport et al. (2020) baseline (Script 6a) applies fixed antecedent-window rain and melt accumulation thresholds directly from that study. The adaptive window scheme (Script 6b) is the primary classification method: for each peak, a single rain fraction metric (`rain_frac`, weighted rain fraction over the peak's site-specific `search_radius` days) is computed from the WLDAS accumulation curves. Diagnostic analysis confirmed that `rain_frac` over the short `search_radius` window is sufficient for classification across all flood types; a longer snowmelt window was investigated and found to be both redundant and potentially harmful due to bleeding across independent events (Section 3.5). Peaks are assigned to one of four types --- Rainfall, Snowmelt, Rain-on-Snow (ROS), or Unclassified --- via a sequential decision tree. A quartile-based scheme (Script 6c) assigns data-sufficient peaks to population-level `rain_frac` quartiles; however, the near-universal bimodal structure of within-site `rain_frac` distributions at Colorado gauges (mass concentrated near 0 and near 1) means Q2 and Q3 are structurally sparse in practice.

## 1. Unclassified Events Under Davenport Thresholds

This chunk characterizes the rate and reasons for unclassified events produced by
the Davenport et al. (2020) threshold-based classification scheme. Two sources of
`flood_type == "unclassified"` exist in the output; this analysis focuses
exclusively on **threshold-level failures** — events where `flood_type_raw ==
"unclassified"` — and excludes peaks demoted to unclassified solely due to the
Yu et al. (2022) minimum sample size filter (n < 20 per type).

```{r load-data}
peaks <- readRDS("../../_data/pot_peaks_classified_davenport.rds")
```

```{r unclassified-reasons}
# Threshold constants (must match 6a_classify_usgs_unit_data_peaks_davenport.R)
RAIN_HIGH <- 10
RAIN_LOW  <-  5
MELT_HIGH <- 10
MELT_LOW  <-  5

# Assign unclassified reason based on antecedent window values.
# Only peaks where flood_type_raw == "unclassified" receive a reason;
# classified peaks and sample-size demotions are kept separate.
peaks <- peaks %>%
  mutate(
    unclassified_reason = case_when(
      flood_type_raw != "unclassified"                        ~ NA_character_,
      !complete_window                                        ~ "incomplete_window",
      total_rain_mm <= RAIN_LOW & total_melt_mm <= MELT_LOW  ~ "below_both_thresholds",
      total_rain_mm > RAIN_LOW  & total_melt_mm <= MELT_LOW &
        total_rain_mm <= RAIN_HIGH                            ~ "rain_ambiguous_zone",
      total_melt_mm > MELT_LOW  & total_rain_mm <= RAIN_LOW &
        total_melt_mm <= MELT_HIGH                            ~ "melt_ambiguous_zone",
      TRUE                                                    ~ "other"
    ),
    # Three-way status for summary tables
    peak_status = case_when(
      flood_type_raw == "unclassified"                        ~ "threshold_unclassified",
      flood_type     == "unclassified"                        ~ "sample_size_demoted",
      TRUE                                                    ~ "classified"
    )
  )
```

```{r summary-all-peaks}
# --- Overall classification status (all POT peaks) ---
status_all <- peaks %>%
  count(peak_status) %>%
  mutate(pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1)) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))

knitr::kable(
  status_all,
  col.names = c("Status", "N", "%"),
  caption   = "Table 1. Classification status across all POT peaks."
)
```

```{r summary-type-all}
# --- Flood type breakdown among truly classified peaks (all POT peaks) ---
type_all <- peaks %>%
  filter(peak_status == "classified") %>%
  count(flood_type) %>%
  mutate(pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1)) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))

knitr::kable(
  type_all,
  col.names = c("Flood type", "N", "%"),
  caption   = "Table 2. Flood type distribution among classified POT peaks."
)
```

```{r reasons-all-peaks}
# --- Unclassified reason breakdown (all POT peaks, threshold failures only) ---
reasons_all <- peaks %>%
  filter(peak_status == "threshold_unclassified") %>%
  count(unclassified_reason) %>%
  mutate(pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1)) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))

knitr::kable(
  reasons_all,
  col.names = c("Reason", "N", "%"),
  caption   = "Table 3. Reasons for threshold-level unclassified peaks (all POT peaks)."
)
```

```{r summary-top-n}
# --- Repeat for top-n subset (in_single_sample == TRUE) ---
peaks_topn <- peaks %>% filter(in_single_sample)

status_topn <- peaks_topn %>%
  count(peak_status) %>%
  mutate(pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1)) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))

knitr::kable(
  status_topn,
  col.names = c("Status", "N", "%"),
  caption   = "Table 4. Classification status among top-n single-sample peaks."
)
```

```{r summary-type-top-n}
# --- Flood type breakdown among classified top-n peaks ---
type_topn <- peaks_topn %>%
  filter(peak_status == "classified") %>%
  count(flood_type) %>%
  mutate(pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1)) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))

knitr::kable(
  type_topn,
  col.names = c("Flood type", "N", "%"),
  caption   = "Table 5. Flood type distribution among classified top-n peaks."
)
```

Note: the top-n single-sample pool contains no threshold-unclassified peaks by
construction — `in_single_sample` is only assigned to peaks that passed the
Davenport thresholds, so a reason breakdown is not applicable for this subset.

```{r threshold-space-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6}
# Scatterplot of all POT peaks in (total_rain_mm, total_melt_mm) space,
# colored by flood_type_raw. A small offset is added before log-scaling to
# handle zero values (common when one forcing is entirely absent).
OFFSET <- 0.1

color_set <- qualitative_hcl(n = 3, palette = "Dark 3")

type_colors <- c(
  "rainfall"      = color_set[1],
  "snowmelt"      = color_set[3],
  "rain_on_snow"  = color_set[2],
  "unclassified"  = "grey70"
)

type_labels <- c(
  "rainfall"      = "Rainfall",
  "snowmelt"      = "Snowmelt",
  "rain_on_snow"  = "Rain-on-snow",
  "unclassified"  = "Unclassified"
)

plot_data <- peaks %>%
  filter(!is.na(total_rain_mm), !is.na(total_melt_mm)) %>%
  mutate(
    rain_plot = total_rain_mm + OFFSET,
    melt_plot = total_melt_mm + OFFSET,
    flood_type_raw = factor(flood_type_raw,
                            levels = c("rainfall", "snowmelt",
                                       "rain_on_snow", "unclassified"))
  ) %>%
  # plot unclassified first so classified points render on top
  arrange(desc(flood_type_raw))

p_thresh_space <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = rain_plot, y = melt_plot, color = flood_type_raw)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.4) +
  # Davenport threshold boundaries
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(5, 10) + OFFSET, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(5, 10) + OFFSET, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_x_log10(
    name   = "Total antecedent rain (mm, log scale)",
    breaks = c(0.1, 1, 5, 10, 50, 100, 200) + OFFSET,
    labels = c(0, 1, 5, 10, 50, 100, 200)
  ) +
  scale_y_log10(
    name   = "Total antecedent snowmelt (mm, log scale)",
    breaks = c(0.1, 1, 5, 10, 50, 100, 200) + OFFSET,
    labels = c(0, 1, 5, 10, 50, 100, 200)
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = type_colors, labels = type_labels,
                     name = "Flood type") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "right") +
  labs(
    title   = "POT peaks in antecedent rain-snowmelt space",
    subtitle = "Dashed lines show Davenport et al. (2020) classification thresholds (5 mm, 10 mm)"
  )

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "01_davenport_threshold_space.png"),
       p_thresh_space, width = 7, height = 6, dpi = 150)
p_thresh_space
```

## 2. The Case Against a Fixed Antecedent Window

The Davenport et al. (2020) classification scheme uses a fixed 8-day antecedent
window to accumulate rain and snowmelt totals prior to each flood peak. This
window was chosen to capture the full precipitation-to-runoff lag for most
western US watersheds, but it does not account for the fact that hydrologic
response time scales vary systematically with basin size. A small headwater
catchment responds to precipitation in hours; a large basin may take many days.
Using the same 8-day window for both conflates the forcing signals of events
that are physically distinct in their timing.

The Livneh et al. (2024) peak independence criterion provides a principled
alternative. The minimum separation between independent peaks is defined as:

$$\theta = 5 + \ln(1.6092 \times A)$$

where $A$ is drainage area in km². This formula encodes the same physical
intuition — larger basins have longer memory — and was used in Script 3 to
decluster POT peaks. We adopt $\theta$ (rounded up to the nearest integer) as
the antecedent accumulation window in the adaptive classification scheme
(Script 6b), so that the window defining event independence also defines the
window over which antecedent forcing is measured.

```{r search-radius-setup}
peaks_raw <- readRDS("../../_data/pot_peaks_all.rds")
metadata  <- readRDS("../../_data/site_metadata.rds")
accum     <- readRDS("../../_data/accum_curves_60d.rds")

# One search radius per site
site_windows <- peaks_raw %>%
  distinct(site_no, search_radius) %>%
  left_join(metadata %>% select(site_no, drain_sqkm), by = "site_no") %>%
  filter(!is.na(drain_sqkm), !is.na(search_radius))

# Theoretical curve from Livneh et al. formula
curve_df <- tibble(
  drain_sqkm    = exp(seq(log(min(site_windows$drain_sqkm)),
                          log(max(site_windows$drain_sqkm)),
                          length.out = 300)),
  search_radius = ceiling(5 + log(1.6092 * drain_sqkm))
)
```

```{r plot-search-radius-vs-area, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 5}
p_sr <- ggplot(site_windows, aes(x = drain_sqkm, y = search_radius)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey50", size = 1.8, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(data = curve_df, color = "#2C7BB6", linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_x_log10(
    name   = expression("Drainage area (km"^2*")"),
    labels = scales::comma
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name   = "Search radius (days)",
    breaks = seq(0, ceiling(max(site_windows$search_radius) / 5) * 5, by = 5)
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title    = "Site-specific antecedent windows vs. drainage area",
    subtitle = expression(theta == "5 + ln(1.6092" %*% "A)   [Livneh et al. 2024]")
  )

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "00_search_radius_vs_area.png"),
       p_sr, width = 6.5, height = 4, dpi = 150)
p_sr
```

Across Colorado sites, $\theta$ ranges from roughly 8 to 17 days, with most
sites falling between 10 and 15 days — well above the Davenport fixed window.
For any site where $\theta > 8$, the Davenport scheme discards antecedent
forcing information that the independence criterion itself treats as
hydrologically relevant. The question is whether this discarded signal is
meaningful in practice.

To assess this, we use 60-day accumulation curves that track cumulative rainfall
and snowmelt day-by-day back from each peak. We focus on "end-member" peaks:
those where the 60-day totals place them unambiguously in the high-rain/low-melt
or high-melt/low-rain corners of the joint distribution. These are the peaks
for which the Davenport thresholds should work best in principle, making them a
conservative test of window adequacy.

```{r accum-endmembers}
# Reproduce end-member classification from accum_curves diagnostic script.
# Using the same percentile cutoffs: primary signal >= 50th, opposing <= 25th.
PRIMARY_PCTILE   <- 0.50
ENDMEMBER_PCTILE <- 0.25

totals_60d <- accum %>%
  filter(lookback_day == 60) %>%
  select(site_no, peak_id, peak_date, peak_flow,
         total_rain_60d = cumul_rain_mm,
         total_melt_60d = cumul_melt_mm,
         n_days_data) %>%
  filter(n_days_data >= 57)

rain_low_cut  <- quantile(totals_60d$total_rain_60d, ENDMEMBER_PCTILE, na.rm = TRUE)
rain_high_cut <- quantile(totals_60d$total_rain_60d, 1 - PRIMARY_PCTILE, na.rm = TRUE)
melt_low_cut  <- quantile(totals_60d$total_melt_60d, ENDMEMBER_PCTILE, na.rm = TRUE)
melt_high_cut <- quantile(totals_60d$total_melt_60d, 1 - PRIMARY_PCTILE, na.rm = TRUE)

totals_60d <- totals_60d %>%
  mutate(
    endmember_type = case_when(
      total_rain_60d >= rain_high_cut & total_melt_60d <= melt_low_cut ~ "rain",
      total_melt_60d >= melt_high_cut & total_rain_60d <= rain_low_cut ~ "melt",
      TRUE                                                              ~ "neither"
    )
  )

em_peaks <- totals_60d %>%
  filter(endmember_type != "neither") %>%
  select(site_no, peak_id, endmember_type)
```

```{r plot-accum-curves, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.5}
accum_summary <- accum %>%
  inner_join(em_peaks, by = c("site_no", "peak_id")) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(cumul_rain_mm, cumul_melt_mm),
               names_to  = "variable",
               values_to = "cumul_mm") %>%
  mutate(variable = if_else(variable == "cumul_rain_mm", "Rainfall", "Snowmelt")) %>%
  group_by(endmember_type, variable, lookback_day) %>%
  summarise(
    median_cumul = median(cumul_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    q25_cumul    = quantile(cumul_mm, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    q75_cumul    = quantile(cumul_mm, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups      = "drop"
  )

em_labels  <- c(rain = "Rain end-members", melt = "Melt end-members")
var_colors <- qualitative_hcl(n = 2, palette = "Dark 3")
names(var_colors) <- c("Rainfall", "Snowmelt")

p_accum <- ggplot(accum_summary,
       aes(x = lookback_day, y = median_cumul,
           color = variable, fill = variable)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q25_cumul, ymax = q75_cumul),
              alpha = 0.15, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 8, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 10, linetype = "dotted",
             color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = 8.5, y = Inf, vjust = 1.5, hjust = 0,
           label = "8-day window", color = "grey30", size = 3.2) +
  annotate("text", x = 59, y = 11.5, hjust = 1,
           label = "10 mm threshold", color = "grey30", size = 3.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = var_colors, name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values  = var_colors, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Lookback days (1 = peak day)",
                     breaks = c(1, 8, 15, 30, 45, 60)) +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Cumulative depth (mm)") +
  facet_wrap(~ endmember_type, ncol = 1,
             labeller = labeller(endmember_type = em_labels)) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top") +
  labs(
    title    = "60-day accumulation curves for end-member peaks",
    subtitle = "Median +/- IQR. Dashed = 8-day window; dotted = 10 mm Davenport threshold."
  )

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "00b_accum_curves_endmembers.png"),
       p_accum, width = 7, height = 5.5, dpi = 150)
p_accum
```

At the median, the 8-day window is not the binding constraint: melt end-members
accumulate roughly 50 mm of snowmelt by day 8, well above the 10 mm Davenport
threshold. The IQR ribbons tell a more nuanced story, however — the lower
quartile of snowmelt accumulation for melt end-members remains near 10 mm
through the first several weeks, meaning a meaningful fraction of these peaks
are at the classification margin even though they are unambiguously
melt-dominated over the full 60-day record.

```{r plot-threshold-exceedance, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4.5}
sr_lookup <- peaks_raw %>%
  distinct(site_no, peak_id = as.character(peak_id), search_radius)

depth_at_windows <- accum %>%
  inner_join(em_peaks, by = c("site_no", "peak_id")) %>%
  left_join(sr_lookup, by = c("site_no", "peak_id")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(search_radius)) %>%
  filter(
    lookback_day == 8 |
    lookback_day == 14 |
    lookback_day == 21 |
    lookback_day == search_radius
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    window_label = case_when(
      lookback_day == 8             ~ "8-day\n(Davenport)",
      lookback_day == 14            ~ "14-day",
      lookback_day == 21            ~ "21-day",
      lookback_day == search_radius ~ "Site-specific\n(theta)"
    ),
    window_label = factor(window_label,
                          levels = c("8-day\n(Davenport)", "14-day",
                                     "21-day", "Site-specific\n(theta)"))
  ) %>%
  distinct(site_no, peak_id, endmember_type, window_label,
           cumul_rain_mm, cumul_melt_mm)

exceedance <- depth_at_windows %>%
  filter(endmember_type == "melt") %>%
  group_by(window_label) %>%
  summarise(
    Rainfall = round(100 * mean(cumul_rain_mm > 10, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    Snowmelt = round(100 * mean(cumul_melt_mm > 10, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    .groups  = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(Rainfall, Snowmelt),
               names_to  = "variable",
               values_to = "pct_above")

p_exceed <- ggplot(exceedance, aes(x = window_label, y = pct_above, fill = variable)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 50, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = var_colors, name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(name   = "% of peaks exceeding 10 mm",
                     limits = c(0, 100), breaks = seq(0, 100, 20)) +
  scale_x_discrete(name = "Accumulation window") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top") +
  labs(
    title    = "Davenport threshold exceedance rate for melt end-members",
    subtitle = "% of melt end-member peaks where cumulative depth exceeds 10 mm at each window length."
  )

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "00c_threshold_exceedance.png"),
       p_exceed, width = 6.5, height = 4.5, dpi = 150)
p_exceed
```

The exceedance rate for snowmelt among melt end-members rises from roughly 45%
at 8 days to a peak of around 65% at 21 days, before settling back to
approximately 55% at the site-specific $\theta$. Two conclusions follow. First,
window length does matter at the margin: nearly one in five additional melt
end-member peaks cross the 10 mm threshold when the window is extended from 8
to 21 days. Second, and more fundamentally, even with an extended window a
substantial fraction of melt end-members never exceed the snowmelt threshold ---
pointing to a limitation that window length alone cannot fix. The Davenport
scheme's strict opposing-signal requirement (rain < 5 mm for a snowmelt
classification) is even more binding, since it appears that rainfall is very
frequently coincident with melting. Extending the window only helps peaks that are
genuinely melt-dominated but accumulate slowly; it cannot recover peaks that
are flagged as ambiguous because of concurrent rainfall. This motivates the
rain-fraction framing of the adaptive classifier, which replaces the binary
threshold logic with a continuous measure of process dominance. Section 3
documents the adaptive classifier in full, including empirical justification for
the choice of `search_radius` as the sole accumulation window.

## 3. The Adaptive Classifier

### 3.1 Feature Engineering

The Davenport scheme classifies peaks using raw cumulative totals --- millimetres
of rain and millimetres of snowmelt accumulated over a fixed window. This works
reasonably well for unambiguous end-members but has two weaknesses. First, a
fixed absolute threshold (e.g., 10 mm snowmelt) has different discriminating
power across basins with very different climatological flux magnitudes: 10 mm
is a meaningful melt signal at a low-elevation rainfall-dominated site but
unremarkable at a high-elevation site where 50 mm of melt in 8 days is routine.
Second, raw totals are sensitive to window length in a way that affects the two
process types asymmetrically, as shown in Section 2.

The adaptive classifier replaces raw totals with a single scale-invariant metric:
the *weighted rain fraction* (`rain_frac`), defined as the fraction of total active flux
attributable to rainfall over the `search_radius` window:

$$\text{rain\_frac} = \frac{\sum_{d=1}^{W} \tilde{r}_d}{\sum_{d=1}^{W} (\tilde{r}_d + \tilde{m}_d)}$$

where $\tilde{r}_d$ and $\tilde{m}_d$ are rainfall and snowmelt on day $d$,
set to zero if below a noise floor of `NOISE_FLOOR_MM` = 0.1 mm/day. Days
below the noise floor are treated as inactive and contribute nothing to either
the numerator or denominator. This prevents trace fluxes --- numerical artefacts
or sub-threshold drizzle --- from distorting the rain fraction on otherwise
quiescent days. The result is bounded on [0, 1] and directly comparable across
basins regardless of climatological flux magnitude.

An earlier design included a longer snowmelt window (`SNOW_MULT × search_radius`
days) and a co-occurrence metric (`ros_flux_frac`). Diagnostic analysis showed
that the longer window is both redundant and potentially harmful --- snowmelt
classification fractions are flat across window multipliers 1x--5x, while upper
outliers in `rain_frac` grow with multiplier length, consistent with bleeding
into adjacent independent events (Section 3.5). A separate co-occurrence metric
is also unnecessary: because `rain_frac` is defined as rain / (rain + melt), any
event reaching the ROS branch already has meaningful contributions from both
fluxes by construction. The classifier therefore uses `rain_frac` over
`search_radius` as its sole feature.

```{r load-classified}
dav  <- readRDS("../../_data/pot_peaks_classified_davenport.rds")
adap <- readRDS("../../_data/pot_peaks_classified_adaptive.rds")

# Consistent type color palette
color_set  <- qualitative_hcl(n = 3, palette = "Dark 3")
type_colors <- c(
  "rainfall"     = color_set[1],
  "snowmelt"     = color_set[3],
  "rain_on_snow" = color_set[2],
  "ROS"          = color_set[2],
  "unclassified" = "grey80"
)
```

### 3.2 Decision Tree

The decision tree is evaluated in order for each peak. `rain_frac` is the sole
classification feature.

1. **Unclassified** --- if `data_sufficient` is FALSE (fewer than 90% of
   `search_radius` days have WLDAS data, or total active flux is below 1 mm),
   the peak is immediately set aside. Classification requires a minimum
   evidential basis.

2. **Rainfall** --- if `rain_frac >= 0.95` (`RAIN_EM_THRESH`), the peak is
   classified as rainfall. A rain fraction of 0.95 or above over the short
   window means rainfall accounts for at least 19 of every 20 units of active
   flux in the immediate antecedent period. This is a high-confidence threshold
   that leaves little room for misclassification of mixed events.

3. **Rain-on-Snow (ROS)** --- if `rain_frac > SNOW_EM_THRESH` (i.e., the peak
   does not qualify as snowmelt), the peak is classified as ROS. Because
   `rain_frac` is defined as rain / (rain + melt), any event reaching this
   branch already has meaningful contributions from both rain and melt flux by
   construction; a separate co-occurrence metric is not needed.

4. **Snowmelt** --- if `rain_frac <= 0.10` (`SNOW_EM_THRESH`), the peak is
   classified as snowmelt. A rain fraction at or below 0.10 indicates
   near-complete melt dominance over the antecedent window.

```{r flowchart, fig.align = "center", out.width = "65%"}
# Build flowchart, export to PNG, then embed via include_graphics so

grViz("
digraph classification {

  graph [layout = dot, rankdir = TB, fontname = 'Helvetica', splines = polyline]

  node [fontname = 'Helvetica', fontsize = 14, margin = 0.3]
  edge [fontname = 'Helvetica', fontsize = 12]

  input [label = 'POT peak event\n(n-day antecedent window\nvia search_radius)',
         shape = rectangle, style = filled, fillcolor = '#f0f0f0',
         width = 3.5, penwidth = 1.5]

  d1 [label = 'Data sufficient?\nn_days_data >= 0.90 x search_radius\nAND total flux >= 1.0 mm',
      shape = diamond, style = filled, fillcolor = '#fef9c3',
      width = 4.5, height = 2.0, penwidth = 1.5, fixedsize = true]

  d2 [label = 'rain_frac >= 0.95?',
      shape = diamond, style = filled, fillcolor = '#fef9c3',
      width = 2.5, height = 1.5, penwidth = 1.5, fixedsize = true]

  d3 [label = 'rain_frac <= 0.10?',
      shape = diamond, style = filled, fillcolor = '#fef9c3',
      width = 2.5, height = 1.5, penwidth = 1.5, fixedsize = true]

  t_unc  [label = 'Unclassified',
          shape = ellipse, style = filled, fillcolor = '#cccccc',

  input -> d1

  d2 -> d3     [taillabel = 'No',  labelangle = -45, labeldistance = 2.5]
  d3 -> t_snow [taillabel = 'Yes', labelangle = -45, labeldistance = 2.5]
  d3 -> t_ros  [taillabel = 'No',  labelangle = 45,  labeldistance = 2.5]
}
") %>%
  export_svg() %>%
  charToRaw() %>%
  rsvg_png(file = flowchart_path, width = 800)

knitr::include_graphics(flowchart_path)
```

The ordering of branches 3 and 4 matters. ROS is evaluated before Snowmelt to
prevent misclassification of rain-burst-on-snowmelt events: a peak where a short
intense rainfall pulse drives runoff from a snowpack-covered basin may have a
`rain_frac` just above `SNOW_EM_THRESH` but should not be classified as Snowmelt.
Evaluating ROS first ensures such events are captured as rain-melt co-occurrence
rather than pushed into the snowmelt category. This ordering also removes the
Mixed class that appeared in earlier versions of the tree: peaks that are neither
clearly rainfall nor clearly snowmelt are assigned to ROS, which is a more
physically informative label for intermediate events involving concurrent rain and
melt flux.

### 3.3 Comparison with Davenport

To assess how the adaptive classifier changes the classification landscape, we
join the two output files on `site_no` and `peak_id` and compare
`flood_type_raw` from each — the pre-sample-size-filter classification in both
cases, so the comparison reflects the classifiers themselves rather than
differences in the sample size threshold.

```{r bar-chart}
# ── Classification Composition: Fixed vs. Adaptive (3-class) ──────────────
# Requires: ffa_classification_summary.rds (Script 8 output)

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

ffa_classification_summary <- readRDS("../../_data/ffa_classification_summary.rds")

# Color/label lookups (from app.R)
type_labels <- c(
  rainfall     = "Rainfall",
  snowmelt     = "Snowmelt",
  rain_on_snow = "Rain-on-Snow",
  ROS          = "Rain-on-Snow",
  unclassified = "Unclassified"
)
type_colors <- c(
  "Rainfall"      = "#e41a1c",
  "Rain-on-Snow"  = "#4daf4a",
  "Snowmelt"      = "#377eb8",
  "Unclassified"  = "#cccccc"
)
method_labels <- c(
  davenport = "Fixed",
  adaptive  = "Adaptive (3-class)"
)
stack_order <- c("Unclassified", "Snowmelt", "Rain-on-Snow", "Rainfall")

plot_df <- ffa_classification_summary %>%
  filter(
    !regulated,                                    # unregulated only; drop if you want both
    method %in% c("davenport", "adaptive")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    flood_label  = dplyr::recode(flood_type, !!!type_labels),
    method_label = factor(dplyr::recode(method, !!!method_labels),
                          levels = unname(method_labels))
  ) %>%
  group_by(method_label, flood_label) %>%
  summarise(n_peaks = sum(n_peaks, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(method_label) %>%
  mutate(frac = n_peaks / sum(n_peaks)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(flood_label = factor(flood_label,
                              levels = stack_order[stack_order %in% unique(flood_label)]))

p_composition <- ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = method_label, y = frac, fill = flood_label)) +
  geom_col(position = position_stack(reverse = FALSE),
           width = 0.55, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.03))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = type_colors, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Fraction of all peaks",
       title = "Classification Composition by Method") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    legend.position    = "right",
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x        = element_text(size = 13),
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "composition_fixed_vs_adaptive.png"), 
       p_composition, width = 6.5, height = 4.5, dpi = 150)
```

```{r single-site-illustration}
# ── FFA Comparison: Fixed vs. Adaptive (3-class), GPD, single site ────────────
# Requires: _data/ffa_curves_gpd.rds, _data/pot_peaks_classified_davenport.rds,
#           _data/pot_peaks_classified_adaptive.rds, functions.R

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(patchwork)
source("../../functions.R")

TARGET_SITE <- "09081600"   # ← change as needed

ffa_curves_gpd <- readRDS("../../_data/ffa_curves_gpd.rds")

type_labels <- c(
  rainfall     = "Rainfall",
  snowmelt     = "Snowmelt",
  rain_on_snow = "Rain-on-Snow",
  ROS          = "Rain-on-Snow",
  non_rainfall = "Non-Rainfall",        # <-- added for 2-class
  unclassified = "Unclassified"
)
type_colors <- c(
  "Rainfall"         = "#e41a1c",
  "Rain-on-Snow"     = "#4daf4a",
  "Snowmelt"         = "#377eb8",
  "Non-Rainfall"     = "#7b3294",       # <-- added for 2-class
  "Single Sample"    = "#888888",
  "Mixture"          = "black",
  "In Single Sample" = "#888888",
  "Unclassified"     = "#cccccc"
)
MIN_SINGLE_SAMPLE <- 25L

# ── Helper: build one FFA ggplot from precomputed curves + raw peaks ──────────
make_ffa_plot <- function(site_no, method_key, method_label,
                          ffa_curves_gpd, peaks_rds_path,
                          ylim = NULL,
                          reclassify_2class = FALSE) {   # <-- new argument

  curves <- ffa_curves_gpd %>%
    filter(site_no == !!site_no, method == method_key) %>%
    mutate(
      label = case_when(
        curve_type == "mixture"       ~ "Mixture",
        curve_type == "single_sample" ~ "Single Sample",
        TRUE                          ~ type_labels[curve_type]
      ),
      color = case_when(
        curve_type == "mixture"       ~ "black",
        curve_type == "single_sample" ~ type_colors["Single Sample"],
        TRUE                          ~ type_colors[type_labels[curve_type]]
      )
    )

  if (nrow(curves) == 0) stop("No curves found for site ", site_no, " / ", method_key)

  peaks <- readRDS(peaks_rds_path) %>%
    filter(site_no == !!site_no, is.finite(peak_flow), peak_flow > 0)

  # Re-label ROS + snowmelt -> non_rainfall so empirical points match curve types
  if (reclassify_2class) {
    peaks <- peaks %>%
      mutate(flood_type = case_when(
        as.character(flood_type_raw) %in% c("ROS", "snowmelt") ~ "non_rainfall",
        as.character(flood_type_raw) == "rainfall"             ~ "rainfall",
        TRUE                                                   ~ "unclassified"
      ))
  }

  type_curve_types <- unique(curves$curve_type[
    !curves$curve_type %in% c("mixture", "single_sample")
  ])

  emp_peaks <- peaks %>%
    filter(as.character(flood_type) %in% type_curve_types, in_type_sample)

  emp <- if (nrow(emp_peaks) > 0) {
    empirical_ri(emp_peaks %>% mutate(flood_type = factor(flood_type))) %>%
      mutate(flood_label = type_labels[as.character(flood_type)])
  } else data.frame()

  if (nrow(emp) > 0 && "single_sample" %in% curves$curve_type) {
    ss_ids <- peaks %>%
      mutate(n    = pmax(MIN_SINGLE_SAMPLE, n_distinct(water_year)),
             rank = row_number(desc(peak_flow))) %>%
      filter(rank <= n) %>%
      pull(peak_flow)
    emp <- emp %>% mutate(in_ss = peak_flow %in% ss_ids)
  } else if (nrow(emp) > 0) {
    emp <- emp %>% mutate(in_ss = FALSE)
  }
  emp_ss <- if (nrow(emp) > 0) filter(emp, in_ss) else data.frame()

  color_vec <- curves %>% distinct(label, color) %>%
    { setNames(.$color, .$label) }
  lty_vec <- setNames(
    ifelse(names(color_vec) %in% c("Mixture", "Single Sample"), "solid", "dashed"),
    names(color_vec)
  )

  ss_label        <- "In Single Sample"
  color_vec_p     <- if (nrow(emp_ss) > 0) c(color_vec, setNames("#888888", ss_label)) else color_vec
  legend_breaks   <- if (nrow(emp_ss) > 0) c(names(color_vec), ss_label) else names(color_vec)
  line_only       <- c("Mixture", "Single Sample")
  shape_overrides <- case_when(
    legend_breaks == ss_label     ~ 1L,
    legend_breaks %in% line_only  ~ NA_integer_,
    TRUE                          ~ 16L
  )

  ggplot() +
    geom_line(data = curves,
              aes(x = ri, y = discharge_cfs, colour = label, linetype = label),
              linewidth = 1.1, na.rm = TRUE) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 100, linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.5, color = "black") +
    { if (nrow(emp_ss) > 0)
        geom_point(data = emp_ss,
                   aes(x = ri, y = peak_flow, colour = ss_label),
                   shape = 1, size = 3.5, stroke = 0.9, alpha = 0.8) } +
    { if (nrow(emp) > 0)
        geom_point(data = emp,
                   aes(x = ri, y = peak_flow, colour = flood_label),
                   shape = 16, size = 1.8, alpha = 0.7) } +
    scale_x_log10(breaks = c(2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 500)) +
    scale_y_log10(labels = label_comma(), limits = ylim) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = color_vec_p, breaks = legend_breaks, name = NULL) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = lty_vec, guide = "none") +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2, override.aes = list(shape = shape_overrides))) +
    labs(title = method_label,
         x = "Return Period (years)", y = "Peak Discharge (cfs)") +
    theme_bw(base_size = 13) +
    theme(
      legend.position  = "bottom",
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5)
    )
}

# ── Helper: compute shared y-limits for a given pair of methods ───────────────
make_ylim <- function(ffa_curves_gpd, site_no, methods) {
  ffa_curves_gpd %>%
    filter(site_no == !!site_no,
           method  %in% methods,
           is.finite(discharge_cfs), discharge_cfs > 0) %>%
    pull(discharge_cfs) %>%
    range() * c(0.9, 1.1)
}

# ── Plot 1: Fixed vs. Adaptive (3-class) ──────────────────────────────────────
ylim_1 <- make_ylim(ffa_curves_gpd, TARGET_SITE, c("davenport", "adaptive"))

p_fixed <- make_ffa_plot(
  TARGET_SITE, "davenport", "Fixed",
  ffa_curves_gpd,
  "../../_data/pot_peaks_classified_davenport.rds",
  ylim = ylim_1
)
p_adaptive_3 <- make_ffa_plot(
  TARGET_SITE, "adaptive", "Adaptive (3-class)",
  ffa_curves_gpd,
  "../../_data/pot_peaks_classified_adaptive.rds",
  ylim = ylim_1
)

p_combined_1 <- p_fixed + p_adaptive_3 +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = paste0("Station ", TARGET_SITE, " — GPD Flood Frequency Analysis"),
    subtitle = "Fixed Threshold vs. Adaptive (3-class) classification",
    theme    = theme(
      plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, colour = "grey40")
    )
  )

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "ffa_comparison_fixed_vs_adaptive.png"),
       p_combined_1, width = 14, height = 7.5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")

# ── Plot 2: Adaptive (3-class) vs. Adaptive (2-class) ────────────────────────
ylim_2 <- make_ylim(ffa_curves_gpd, TARGET_SITE, c("adaptive", "adaptive_2class"))

p_adaptive_2 <- make_ffa_plot(
  TARGET_SITE, "adaptive_2class", "Adaptive (2-class)",
  ffa_curves_gpd,
  "../../_data/pot_peaks_classified_adaptive.rds",
  ylim              = ylim_2,
  reclassify_2class = TRUE
)
p_adaptive_3b <- make_ffa_plot(
  TARGET_SITE, "adaptive", "Adaptive (3-class)",
  ffa_curves_gpd,
  "../../_data/pot_peaks_classified_adaptive.rds",
  ylim = ylim_2
)

p_combined_2 <- p_adaptive_3b + p_adaptive_2 +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = paste0("Station ", TARGET_SITE, " — GPD Flood Frequency Analysis"),
    subtitle = "Adaptive (3-class) vs. Adaptive (2-class) classification",
    theme    = theme(
      plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, colour = "grey40")
    )
  )

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "ffa_comparison_adaptive_3v2.png"),
       p_combined_2, width = 14, height = 7.5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

```{r cross-classify}
# Join on site_no and peak_id; keep pre-filter classifications only
cross <- dav %>%
  select(site_no, peak_id, dav_type = flood_type_raw) %>%
  inner_join(
    adap %>% select(site_no, peak_id, adap_type = flood_type_raw),
    by = c("site_no", "peak_id")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    dav_type  = factor(as.character(dav_type),
                       levels = c("rainfall", "snowmelt", "rain_on_snow",
                                  "unclassified")),
    adap_type = factor(as.character(adap_type),
                       levels = c("rainfall", "snowmelt", "ROS",
                                  "unclassified"))
  )

# Cross-classification table: row = Davenport, col = adaptive
ct <- cross %>%
  count(dav_type, adap_type) %>%
  group_by(dav_type) %>%
  mutate(row_pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1)) %>%
  ungroup()

ct_wide <- ct %>%
  mutate(cell = sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", n, row_pct)) %>%
  select(dav_type, adap_type, cell) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = adap_type, values_from = cell, values_fill = "0 (0.0%)")

knitr::kable(
  ct_wide,
  col.names = c("Davenport type", "Rainfall", "Snowmelt", "ROS", "Unclassified"),
  caption   = paste0(
    "Cross-classification of POT peaks by Davenport (rows) and adaptive (columns) ",
    "schemes. Pre-sample-size-filter classifications. Row percentages in parentheses."
  ),
  align = c("l", rep("r", 5))
)
```


The cross-classification table reveals where the two schemes agree and diverge.
Peaks that Davenport assigns to rainfall are expected to map predominantly to
the adaptive rainfall category, since both schemes require a strong rainfall
signal over the short antecedent window --- the difference is that the adaptive
scheme uses a continuous rain fraction rather than a 10 mm absolute threshold.
The more instructive rows are Davenport's unclassified peaks: these are events
that fell into the ambiguous zone between thresholds, and the table shows how
many of them the adaptive scheme is able to resolve into rainfall, snowmelt,
or ROS, and how many remain unclassified due to data insufficiency.

The density plot shows the marginal distribution of `rain_frac` by flood type.
Rainfall peaks are concentrated at the right end (near 1.0), and snowmelt peaks
at the left end (near 0), consistent with the end-member threshold design.
ROS peaks occupy the intermediate region. The decision boundaries at
`rain_frac = 0.95` and `rain_frac = 0.10` are shown as dashed lines.

### 3.4 Threshold Justification

The choices of `RAIN_EM_THRESH = 0.95` and `SNOW_EM_THRESH = 0.10` were evaluated against two complementary criteria: whether the threshold sits in a sparse region of the `rain_frac` distribution (a density-based test for a natural boundary), and whether GPD shape parameter estimates for the affected flood type are stable across a range of candidate threshold values (a stability test). All diagnostics use unregulated sites only and operate on `rain_frac` values from `pot_peaks_classified_adaptive.rds`, so no recomputation from raw WLDAS data is required.

```{r diag-setup}
classified <- readRDS("../../_data/pot_peaks_classified_adaptive.rds")
meta        <- readRDS("../../_data/site_metadata.rds")
peak_meta   <- readRDS("../../_data/pot_peaks_all.rds") %>%
  distinct(site_no, peak_id, search_radius, pot_threshold_cfs)

unreg_sites  <- meta %>% filter(!regulated) %>% pull(site_no)
mu_lookup    <- peak_meta %>%
  group_by(site_no) %>%
  summarise(pot_threshold_cfs = first(pot_threshold_cfs), .groups = "drop")

peaks_unreg <- classified %>%
  filter(site_no %in% unreg_sites, data_sufficient, !is.na(rain_frac))

# GPD xi helper
fit_gpd_xi <- function(flows, mu, min_n = MIN_TYPE_SAMPLE) {
  if (length(flows) < min_n) return(NA_real_)
  x <- flows[flows > mu] - mu
  if (length(x) < min_n) return(NA_real_)
  lmom <- tryCatch(lmomco::lmoms(x), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(lmom)) return(NA_real_)
  pars <- tryCatch(lmomco::pargpa(lmom), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(pars) || is.null(pars$para)) return(NA_real_)
  unname(pars$para["xi"])
}
```

#### Rainfall threshold (RAIN_EM_THRESH = 0.95)

The first figure shows the `rain_frac` density restricted to the candidate range (0.70--0.95), with the chosen threshold marked. The second shows GPD $\xi$ for the rainfall type across the same range.

```{r rain-thresh-density, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4, out.width = "100%"}
p02a
```

```{r rain-thresh-stability, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4, out.width = "100%"}
# 02b: GPD xi stability across rainfall threshold scan
rain_thresholds <- seq(0.70, 0.99, by = 0.01)

rain_xi_results <- map_dfr(rain_thresholds, function(thr) {
  peaks_unreg %>%
    filter(rain_frac >= thr) %>%
    group_by(site_no) %>%
    arrange(desc(peak_flow), .by_group = TRUE) %>%
    mutate(rank = row_number(), n_site = n()) %>%
    filter(rank <= max(MIN_TYPE_SAMPLE, n_site)) %>%
    filter(n_site >= MIN_TYPE_SAMPLE) %>%
    summarise(
      xi = fit_gpd_xi(peak_flow,
                      mu = mu_lookup$pot_threshold_cfs[mu_lookup$site_no == first(site_no)]),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(threshold = thr)
})

rain_xi_summary <- rain_xi_results %>%
  filter(!is.na(xi)) %>%
  group_by(threshold) %>%
  summarise(
    xi_median = median(xi),
    xi_q25    = quantile(xi, 0.25),
    xi_q75    = quantile(xi, 0.75),
    n_sites   = n(),
    .groups   = "drop"
  )

xi_cv <- rain_xi_summary %>%
  summarise(cv = sd(xi_median) / abs(mean(xi_median))) %>%
  pull(cv)

p02b <- ggplot(rain_xi_summary, aes(x = threshold)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = xi_q25, ymax = xi_q75),
              fill = "#e41a1c", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = xi_median), color = "#e41a1c", linewidth = 1.0) +
  geom_point(aes(y = xi_median), color = "#e41a1c", size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = RAIN_EM_THRESH, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "#333333", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted",
             color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.6) +
  annotate("text", x = RAIN_EM_THRESH - 0.003, y = Inf,
           label = sprintf("%.2f\nCV = %.3f", RAIN_EM_THRESH, xi_cv),
           vjust = 1.5, hjust = 1, size = 3.2) +
  labs(
    title    = "GPD shape parameter (xi) for rainfall type vs. threshold",
    subtitle = "Median +/- IQR across unregulated sites; flat xi = threshold-insensitive",
    x        = "rain_frac threshold (rainfall >= this)",
    y        = expression("GPD shape parameter " * (xi)),
    caption  = sprintf("Sites with >= %d rainfall peaks included at each threshold", MIN_TYPE_SAMPLE)
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "02b_rainfall_gpd_xi_stability.png"),
       p02b, width = 6.5, height = 4, dpi = 150)
p02b
```

`RAIN_EM_THRESH = 0.95` sits in a naturally sparse zone on the ascending shoulder of the rainfall density spike --- the shaded candidate range (0.70--0.95) contains very few peaks relative to the spike above 0.95, indicating the threshold is not cutting through a dense region of the distribution. GPD $\xi$ for the rainfall type is essentially flat across the full 0.70--0.95 range (CV = `r round(xi_cv, 3)`), confirming that rainfall classifications are insensitive to the precise threshold choice in this region. The value 0.95 was retained as the most conservative defensible choice: at least 19 of every 20 flux units must be attributable to rainfall, leaving minimal room for melt contamination.

#### Snowmelt threshold (SNOW_EM_THRESH = 0.10)

The first figure shows the `rain_frac` density at the low end of the non-rainfall population, with the scan range shaded. The second shows GPD $\xi$ for the snowmelt type across candidate threshold values.

```{r snow-thresh-density, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4, out.width = "100%"}
non_rainfall <- peaks_unreg %>% filter(rain_frac < RAIN_EM_THRESH)

# 03a: rain_frac density at the low end
p03a <- ggplot(non_rainfall %>% filter(rain_frac <= 0.30),
               aes(x = rain_frac)) +

    title    = "rain_frac distribution (low end) --- non-rainfall population",

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "03a_snowmelt_threshold_distribution.png"),

```

```{r snow-thresh-stability, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4, out.width = "100%"}
# 03b: GPD xi vs. snowmelt threshold
snow_thresholds <- seq(0.01, 0.20, by = 0.01)

snow_xi_results <- map_dfr(snow_thresholds, function(thr) {
  non_rainfall %>%
    filter(rain_frac <= thr) %>%
    group_by(site_no) %>%
    arrange(desc(peak_flow), .by_group = TRUE) %>%
    mutate(rank = row_number(), n_site = n()) %>%
    filter(rank <= max(MIN_TYPE_SAMPLE, n_site)) %>%
    filter(n_site >= MIN_TYPE_SAMPLE) %>%
    summarise(
      xi = fit_gpd_xi(peak_flow,
                      mu = mu_lookup$pot_threshold_cfs[mu_lookup$site_no == first(site_no)]),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(threshold = thr)
})

snow_xi_summary <- snow_xi_results %>%
  filter(!is.na(xi)) %>%
  group_by(threshold) %>%
  summarise(
    xi_median = median(xi),
    xi_q25    = quantile(xi, 0.25),
    xi_q75    = quantile(xi, 0.75),
    n_sites   = n(),
    .groups   = "drop"
  )

snow_xi_cv <- snow_xi_summary %>%
  summarise(cv = sd(xi_median) / abs(mean(xi_median))) %>%
  pull(cv)

p03b <- ggplot(snow_xi_summary, aes(x = threshold)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = xi_q25, ymax = xi_q75),
              fill = "#377eb8", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = xi_median), color = "#377eb8", linewidth = 1.0) +
  geom_point(aes(y = xi_median), color = "#377eb8", size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = SNOW_EM_THRESH, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "#333333", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted",
             color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.6) +
  annotate("text", x = SNOW_EM_THRESH + 0.003, y = Inf,
           label = sprintf("%.2f\nCV = %.3f", SNOW_EM_THRESH, snow_xi_cv),
           vjust = 1.5, hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = snow_thresholds[seq(1, length(snow_thresholds), 2)]) +
  labs(
    title    = "GPD shape parameter (xi) for snowmelt type vs. threshold",
    subtitle = "Median +/- IQR; xi stabilises around 0.05-0.10 then flattens",
    x        = "rain_frac threshold (snowmelt <= this)",
    y        = expression("GPD shape parameter " * (xi)),
    caption  = sprintf("Sites with >= %d snowmelt peaks included at each threshold", MIN_TYPE_SAMPLE)
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "03b_snowmelt_gpd_xi_stability.png"),
       p03b, width = 6.5, height = 4, dpi = 150)
p03b
```

Unlike the rainfall threshold, there is no density gap supporting a natural snowmelt boundary: the low-fraction mode of `rain_frac` is a continuous hump rather than a bimodal distribution with a trough. The threshold choice is therefore a practical one informed by the GPD stability scan. At very low threshold values (0.01--0.05) $\xi$ is notably more negative and site counts are thin, indicating that an overly strict definition captures too few sites for stable estimation. The sharpest change in both $\xi$ and site count occurs at the 0.05--0.06 transition; above 0.06, $\xi$ continues to drift gradually but acute sample-size volatility subsides. The chosen value of `SNOW_EM_THRESH = 0.10` sits within the stable plateau, providing a margin above the inflection point without admitting peaks where rain contributions are non-trivial.

### 3.5 Window Multiplier Sensitivity

The accumulation curve analysis in Section 2 raised the question of whether a longer window --- scaled from `search_radius` by a multiplier --- would improve snowmelt classification. Two diagnostics address this. First, the fraction of non-rainfall peaks classified as snowmelt at each multiplier quantifies whether window length materially affects which peaks are assigned to snowmelt. Second, the distribution of `rain_frac` values at each multiplier, restricted to peaks classified as snowmelt at 1x, reveals whether values shift as the window expands.

```{r window-multiplier, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4, out.width = "100%"}
MULTIPLIERS    <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
accum          <- readRDS("../../_data/accum_curves_60d.rds")

accum_with_sr <- accum %>%
  inner_join(peak_meta %>% select(site_no, peak_id, search_radius),
             by = c("site_no", "peak_id")) %>%
  filter(site_no %in% unreg_sites)

# Compute rain_frac at each multiplier for all unregulated data-sufficient peaks
rf_by_mult <- map_dfr(MULTIPLIERS, function(m) {
  accum_with_sr %>%
    filter(lookback_day <= m * search_radius) %>%
    mutate(
      rain_active = if_else(rain_mm_day >= NOISE_FLOOR_MM, rain_mm_day, 0),
      melt_active = if_else(melt_mm_day >= NOISE_FLOOR_MM, melt_mm_day, 0),
      total_flux  = rain_active + melt_active
    ) %>%
    group_by(site_no, peak_id) %>%
    summarise(
      rain_flux  = sum(rain_active, na.rm = TRUE),
      total_flux = sum(total_flux,  na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups    = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      rf_mult    = if_else(total_flux > 0, rain_flux / total_flux, NA_real_),
      multiplier = m
    ) %>%
    select(site_no, peak_id, multiplier, rf_mult)
})

rf_mult_peaks <- peaks_unreg %>%
  filter(rain_frac < RAIN_EM_THRESH) %>%
  select(site_no, peak_id) %>%
  inner_join(rf_by_mult, by = c("site_no", "peak_id"))

# 04a: Snowmelt fraction vs. multiplier
snowmelt_frac <- rf_mult_peaks %>%
  filter(!is.na(rf_mult)) %>%
  group_by(multiplier) %>%
  summarise(
    n_total   = n(),
    n_snow    = sum(rf_mult <= SNOW_EM_THRESH),
    frac_snow = n_snow / n_total,
    .groups   = "drop"
  )

p04a <- ggplot(snowmelt_frac, aes(x = multiplier, y = frac_snow)) +
  geom_line(color = "#377eb8", linewidth = 1.0) +
  geom_point(color = "#377eb8", size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%\n(n=%d)", frac_snow * 100, n_snow)),
            vjust = -0.6, size = 3.2, color = "#377eb8") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = MULTIPLIERS,
                     labels = sprintf("%dx", MULTIPLIERS)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 0.1),
                     limits = c(0, max(snowmelt_frac$frac_snow) * 1.15)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Fraction of non-rainfall peaks classified as snowmelt vs. window multiplier",
    subtitle = sprintf("Snowmelt criterion: rain_frac <= %.2f; rainfall end-members excluded",
                       SNOW_EM_THRESH),
    x        = "Window length (multiples of search_radius)",
    y        = "Fraction classified as snowmelt"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "04a_snowmelt_frac_vs_multiplier.png"),
       p04a, width = 6.5, height = 4, dpi = 150)
p04a
```

```{r rain-frac-vs-multiplier, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4, out.width = "100%"}
# 04b: rain_frac distribution by multiplier for peaks snowmelt at 1x
snow_at_1x <- rf_mult_peaks %>%
  filter(multiplier == 1, rf_mult <= SNOW_EM_THRESH) %>%
  select(site_no, peak_id)

rf_snow_wide <- rf_mult_peaks %>%
  semi_join(snow_at_1x, by = c("site_no", "peak_id")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(rf_mult)) %>%
  mutate(multiplier = factor(sprintf("%dx", multiplier),
                             levels = sprintf("%dx", MULTIPLIERS)))

p04b <- ggplot(rf_snow_wide, aes(x = multiplier, y = rf_mult)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#377eb8", alpha = 0.4, outlier.size = 0.8,
               outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = SNOW_EM_THRESH, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.6, y = SNOW_EM_THRESH + 0.005,
           label = sprintf("Snowmelt threshold = %.2f", SNOW_EM_THRESH),
           hjust = 0, vjust = 0, size = 3.2, color = "firebrick") +
  labs(
    title    = "rain_frac distribution vs. window multiplier --- peaks snowmelt at 1x",
    subtitle = "IQR stable below threshold at all multipliers; outliers grow with window length",
    x        = "Window length (multiples of search_radius)",
    y        = "rain_frac at given multiplier",
    caption  = paste0(
      "Peaks classified as snowmelt at 1x search_radius (the Livneh independence window).\n",
      "Growing upper outliers at longer windows are consistent with bleeding into\n",
      "adjacent independent events --- reinforcing search_radius as the correct window."
    )
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "04b_rain_frac_vs_multiplier.png"),
       p04b, width = 6.5, height = 4, dpi = 150)
p04b
```

The snowmelt classification fraction is essentially flat across all multipliers (04a), confirming that extending the window beyond `search_radius` does not materially change which peaks are assigned to snowmelt. The boxplot (04b) explains why: for peaks classified as snowmelt at 1x, the IQR of `rain_frac` remains well below the threshold at every multiplier. What does grow is the upper tail --- outliers increase systematically with multiplier length, consistent with longer windows accumulating flux from adjacent independent events that the Livneh criterion was specifically designed to exclude. A multiplier greater than 1 is therefore not merely redundant but potentially harmful, and `search_radius` (multiplier = 1) is confirmed as both sufficient and appropriate.

## 4. The Rainfall--Snowmelt Divide

The classification analyses in Section 3 document the mechanics of the adaptive
classifier. This section steps back and asks two related questions: does the
`rain_frac` distribution actually support the 3-class schema, and are the
assigned classes physically coherent in joint feature space?

```{r section4-setup}
adap <- readRDS("../../_data/pot_peaks_classified_adaptive.rds")
meta <- readRDS("../../_data/site_metadata.rds")

color_set <- qualitative_hcl(n = 3, palette = "Dark 3")
type_colors <- c(
  "rainfall"     = color_set[1],
  "snowmelt"     = color_set[3],
  "ROS"          = color_set[2],
  "unclassified" = "grey80"
)
type_labels <- c(
  "rainfall"     = "Rainfall",
  "snowmelt"     = "Snowmelt",
  "ROS"          = "Rain-on-snow",
  "unclassified" = "Unclassified"
)

ELEV_BREAKS <- c(0, 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000, Inf)
ELEV_LABELS <- c("< 1500 m", "1500-2000 m", "2000-2500 m",
                 "2500-3000 m", "> 3000 m")

peaks_elev <- adap %>%
  filter(site_no %in% (meta %>% filter(!regulated) %>% pull(site_no)),
         data_sufficient, !is.na(rain_frac)) %>%
  left_join(meta %>% select(site_no, elev_mean_m), by = "site_no") %>%
  mutate(elev_band = cut(elev_mean_m, breaks = ELEV_BREAKS,
                         labels = ELEV_LABELS, right = FALSE))

middle_bin <- peaks_elev %>%
  filter(rain_frac > SNOW_EM_THRESH, rain_frac < RAIN_EM_THRESH)
```

### 4.1 Full Distribution and the 3-Class Schema

The full `rain_frac` distribution is strongly bimodal, with clear end-member
modes near 0 and 1 and a relatively sparse middle region. This motivates a
3-class schema: the two end-members are well-supported by the data, and the
middle bin (ROS) captures the intermediate population without subdividing it
further on a feature where no natural breakpoint exists.

```{r full-distribution, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4, out.width = "100%"}
p01a <- ggplot(peaks_elev, aes(x = rain_frac)) +
  geom_density(fill = "#e41a1c", alpha = 0.25, color = "#e41a1c", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = RAIN_EM_THRESH, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "#e41a1c", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = SNOW_EM_THRESH, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "#377eb8", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = RAIN_EM_THRESH - 0.01, y = Inf,
           label = sprintf("Rainfall\n>= %.2f", RAIN_EM_THRESH),
           vjust = 1.5, hjust = 1, color = "#e41a1c", size = 3.2) +
  annotate("text", x = SNOW_EM_THRESH + 0.01, y = Inf,
           label = sprintf("Snowmelt\n<= %.2f", SNOW_EM_THRESH),
           vjust = 1.5, hjust = 0, color = "#377eb8", size = 3.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.01))) +
  labs(
    title    = "Distribution of antecedent rain fraction",
    subtitle = sprintf("All unregulated data-sufficient peaks",
                       100 * nrow(middle_bin) / nrow(peaks_elev)),
    x        = "Antecedent Rain Fraction",
    y        = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "01a_rain_frac_full_distribution.png"),
       p01a, width = 6.5, height = 4, dpi = 150)
p01a
```

The middle bin contains `r nrow(middle_bin)` peaks
(`r round(100 * nrow(middle_bin) / nrow(peaks_elev), 0)`% of all
data-sufficient unregulated peaks). To assess whether a 4-class split within
this bin would be defensible, we examine the middle-bin distribution by
elevation band. If there were a natural breakpoint separating
snowmelt-dominated ROS from rainfall-dominated ROS, it should be most visible
at high elevations where the melt signal is largest.

```{r middle-bin-elevation, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 5.5, out.width = "100%"}
elev_n <- middle_bin %>%
  dplyr::count(elev_band) %>%
  mutate(label = sprintf("%s\nn = %d", elev_band, n))

middle_bin_labeled <- middle_bin %>%
  left_join(elev_n %>% select(elev_band, label), by = "elev_band")

p01b <- ggplot(middle_bin_labeled, aes(x = rain_frac)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)),
                 binwidth = 0.05, fill = "#7b3294", alpha = 0.55,
                 color = "white") +
  geom_density(color = "#1a1a1a", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.50, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(SNOW_EM_THRESH, RAIN_EM_THRESH),
                     breaks = seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.2)) +
  facet_wrap(~ label, ncol = 3) +
  labs(
    title    = "rain_frac distribution by elevation --- middle bin (ROS)",
    subtitle = "No bimodality at dominant elevations; no natural 4-class breakpoint",
    x        = "rain_frac",
    y        = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0"))

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "01b_middle_bin_by_elevation.png"),
       p01b, width = 6.5, height = 5.5, dpi = 150)
p01b
```

The middle-bin distribution is approximately uniform across all elevation bands
with no bimodal structure. There is no natural breakpoint at any elevation,
confirming that a 4-class split within the ROS bin is not supported by the data
and that the 3-class schema is the appropriate level of granularity.

### 4.2 Classification in Joint Feature Space

To confirm that the three classes occupy physically distinct regions and that
`rain_frac` alone separates them, we plot `rain_frac` against total melt flux
over the antecedent window. A classifier that captures genuine process
differences should show the three types separating cleanly along the `rain_frac`
axis, with melt flux providing an independent second dimension that does not
contradict the classification.

```{r feature-space-scatter, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 5, out.width = "100%"}
type_colors_scatter <- c(
  rainfall = "#e41a1c",
  ROS      = "#7b3294",
  snowmelt = "#377eb8"
)

scatter_df <- peaks_elev %>%
  filter(as.character(flood_type_raw) %in% c("rainfall", "ROS", "snowmelt"),
         melt_flux_short > 0) %>%
  mutate(flood_type_raw = factor(as.character(flood_type_raw),
                                 levels = c("snowmelt", "ROS", "rainfall")))

p01c <- ggplot(scatter_df,
               aes(x = rain_frac, y = melt_flux_short,
                   color = flood_type_raw)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = SNOW_EM_THRESH, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = RAIN_EM_THRESH, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma(),
                breaks  = c(0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000)) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = type_colors_scatter,
    labels = c(snowmelt = "Snowmelt", ROS = "Rain-on-Snow", rainfall = "Rainfall"),
    name   = "Flood type"
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = SNOW_EM_THRESH / 2, y = Inf,
           label = "Snowmelt", vjust = 1.5, color = "#377eb8", size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = (SNOW_EM_THRESH + RAIN_EM_THRESH) / 2, y = Inf,
           label = "ROS", vjust = 1.5, color = "#7b3294", size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = (RAIN_EM_THRESH + 1) / 2, y = Inf,
           label = "Rainfall", vjust = 1.5, color = "#e41a1c", size = 3.5) +
  labs(
    title    = "Classification in feature space --- rain_frac vs. melt flux",
    subtitle = "Dashed lines = classification boundaries; y-axis log scale",
    x        = "rain_frac",
    y        = "Total melt flux over window (mm)"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "01c_feature_space_scatter.png"),
       p01c, width = 6.5, height = 5, dpi = 150)
p01c
```

The three types separate cleanly along the `rain_frac` axis by construction.
The melt flux dimension provides the key additional insight: snowmelt peaks span
a wide range of melt flux values (high melt flux as expected), ROS peaks occupy
the intermediate `rain_frac` range with a broad melt flux distribution, and
rainfall peaks cluster at low melt flux regardless of `rain_frac`. This
confirms that the 3-class assignments are physically coherent --- the
`rain_frac`-based boundaries align with independent variation in melt flux, not
just with the classification labels themselves.

### 4.3 What the Classifier Is and Is Not Doing

Taken together, these figures sharpen what can and cannot be claimed about
the adaptive classification. The rainfall category rests on a genuinely
data-driven boundary: the spike near 1.0 is a real distributional feature,
and the 0.95 threshold captures it cleanly. The snowmelt and ROS categories
do not have the same foundation --- the non-rainfall population shows no
internal discontinuity in `rain_frac` that would support treating them as
naturally distinct populations. The boundary between them is imposed by the
classifier at `SNOW_EM_THRESH = 0.10`, not discovered in the data.

This limitation is more of a practical acknowledgment than a fatal flaw. The
classifier's goal is not to discover unsupervised clusters but to make
defensible, physically motivated assignments for FFA purposes. The rainfall
end-member is well-supported by the data. The snowmelt and ROS assignments are
threshold-based engineering decisions, consistent with the philosophy of
Davenport et al. (2020) and HEC manual typing procedures, made on a continuous
scale rather than from absolute accumulation totals. The value of the
classification lies in whether the assigned types produce statistically
distinguishable flood frequency curves --- a question addressed in the
downstream FFA.

### 5. Peak Magnitude by Process Quartile

The quartile classification in Script 6c assigns every data-sufficient peak to Q1--Q4
based on its position in the population-wide distribution of `rain_frac`. By construction
each quartile contains the same number of peaks globally, but in practice Q3 rarely
produces a sufficient per-site sample to fit a GPD curve while Q2 often does. Two
explanations are possible: a sampling artifact arising from the mismatch between
population-level quartile boundaries and the per-site distribution of `rain_frac`, or a
physical signal in which Q3 peaks are systematically smaller relative to their site's
POT threshold and therefore less likely to survive the top-n filter.

This section examines the latter possibility by comparing the distribution of peak
exceedance ratios — defined as `peak_flow / pot_threshold_cfs` — across Q1–Q4 using
the full data-sufficient population before any top-n filtering.

```{r quartile-exceedance, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4.5}
quart <- readRDS("../../_data/pot_peaks_classified_quartile.rds")

exceedance_df <- quart %>%
  filter(data_sufficient, flood_type != "unclassified",
         is.finite(peak_flow), peak_flow > 0,
         is.finite(pot_threshold_cfs), pot_threshold_cfs > 0) %>%
  mutate(
    exceedance_ratio = peak_flow / pot_threshold_cfs,
    flood_type = factor(flood_type, levels = c("Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"))
  )

quartile_colors <- c(
  Q1 = "#2166ac",
  Q2 = "#92c5de",
  Q3 = "#f4a582",
  Q4 = "#b2182b"
)

quartile_labels <- c(
  Q1 = "Q1\n(melt-dominated)",
  Q2 = "Q2",
  Q3 = "Q3",
  Q4 = "Q4\n(rain-dominated)"
)

p_qexceed <- ggplot(exceedance_df, aes(x = flood_type, y = exceedance_ratio, fill = flood_type)) +
  geom_violin(trim = TRUE, scale = "width", alpha = 0.6, color = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, outlier.shape = NA, fill = "white",
               color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = quartile_labels) +
  scale_y_log10(
    name   = "Peak flow / POT threshold (log scale)",
    breaks = c(1, 2, 5, 10, 25),
    labels = c("1x", "2x", "5x", "10x", "25x")
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = quartile_colors, guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title    = "Peak exceedance ratio by process quartile",
    subtitle = "All data-sufficient peaks before top-n filtering. POT threshold = site-wide GPD mu.",
    x        = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "05a_quartile_exceedance_ratios.png"),
       p_qexceed, width = 6.5, height = 4.5, dpi = 150)
p_qexceed
```

The violin plots show the full distribution of exceedance ratios within each quartile;
the embedded boxplots summarise the median and interquartile range. The distributions
reveal a pattern opposite to the sampling-artifact hypothesis: Q3 has a notably higher
median and fatter upper tail than any other quartile, while Q2 is the most compressed,
with the lowest median and the least mass in the upper tail. Q1 and Q4 are broadly
similar to each other, both sitting between the Q2 and Q3 extremes.

The scarcity of Q3 in per-site top-n samples is therefore unlikely to reflect
systematically smaller peaks. Instead it is more likely a boundary artifact: the
population-level quartile cuts map unevenly onto within-site distributions, and sites
where Q3 peaks are common enough to meet the `MIN_TYPE_SAMPLE` threshold may simply
be rare given the bimodal geography of Colorado flood processes.

The more substantive finding is the Q2 dip. Q2 events occur when rain is present but
melt still dominates the antecedent flux over the long window — conditions characteristic
of the transitional melt season, where both signals contribute but neither drives a sharp
peak. Q1 events are pure melt-dominated and can produce large peaks when snowmelt is
rapid and concentrated. Q3 and Q4 are rain-influenced enough that convective or frontal
precipitation can drive genuine extremes. The result is a non-monotonic relationship
between rain fraction and flood magnitude, with transitional mixed-process events
producing the most modest peaks relative to the POT threshold.

### 5.1 Within-Site Quartile Frequency

If Q3 is absent from most per-site top-n samples despite producing large peaks
globally, the explanation cannot be that Q3 peaks are small — Section 5 showed the
opposite. Nor is it simply that sites narrowly miss the `MIN_TYPE_SAMPLE` threshold:
the heatmap below shows that most sites have close to zero Q3 peaks in the first
place. The population-level quartile construction guarantees equal counts globally by
definition, but makes no guarantee about counts within any individual site. If the
within-site distribution of `rain_frac` is strongly bimodal — with mass concentrated
near 0 and near 1 and a near-empty interior — then a site's peaks will land almost
entirely in Q1 and Q4, with the global Q2 and Q3 intervals filled by contributions
from many sites rather than from any one. The figures below confirm this is the case.

#### Per-site quartile composition

The chart below shows the quartile composition of each site's data-sufficient
peaks. Sites are ordered left to right by increasing median `rain_frac`; each
bar is one site and fill shows the proportion of peaks in each quartile.
Q3 is nearly absent across the full spectrum, confirming that it is
structurally unoccupied at the site level regardless of process dominance.

```{r quartile-site-counts, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4, out.width = "100%"}
adap <- readRDS("../../_data/pot_peaks_classified_adaptive.rds")

# by quartile ----
site_props <- adap %>%
  filter(data_sufficient, !regulated, !is.na(rain_frac)) %>%
  mutate(quartile = ifelse(rain_frac > 0.75, "Q4", 
                                ifelse(rain_frac > 0.5, "Q3", 
                                       ifelse(rain_frac > 0.25, "Q2", 
                                              "Q1")))) %>%
  group_by(site_no, quartile) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(site_no) %>%
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup()

plot_df <- site_props %>%
  mutate(quartile = factor(quartile, levels = c("Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4")))

site_order <- plot_df %>%
  mutate(quartile = factor(quartile, levels = c("Q4", "Q3", "Q2", "Q1"))) %>%
  arrange(quartile, -prop) %>%
  distinct(site_no)

plot_df <- site_props %>%
  mutate(
    site_no  = factor(site_no, levels = site_order$site_no),
    quartile = factor(quartile, levels = c("Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"))
  )

type_colors <- c(Q1 = "#2166ac", Q2 = "#92c5de", Q3 = "#f4a582", Q4 = "#b2182b")

p_type_heat <- ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = site_no, y = prop, fill = quartile)) +
  geom_col(width = 1, color = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = type_colors,
    labels = c(Q1 = "Q1 (<25% rain)", 
               Q2 = "Q2",
               Q3 = "Q3",
               Q4 = "Q4 (>75% rain)"),
    name   = "Rain fraction (per peak)"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1),
                     breaks = c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = 0)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Antecedent rain fraction composition per site",
    subtitle = "Left = most rain-dominated, right = most melt-dominated",
    x        = "Sites ordered by Q4 fraction",
    y        = "Proportion of peaks"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x        = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x       = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    legend.position    = "bottom",
    legend.title.position = "top",
    legend.key.size    = unit(0.4, "cm")
  )

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "05c_adaptive_site_composition_by_quartile.png"),
       p_type_heat, width = 6.5, height = 4, dpi = 150)
p_type_heat

# by flood type ----
site_props <- adap %>%
  filter(data_sufficient, !regulated, !is.na(rain_frac)) %>%
  mutate(class = ifelse(rain_frac > 0.95, "rainfall", 
                                ifelse(rain_frac < 0.2, "snowmelt", 
                                       "ROS"))) %>%
  group_by(site_no, class) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%

  mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup()

plot_df <- site_props %>%
  mutate(class = factor(class, levels = c("snowmelt", "ROS", "rainfall")))

site_order <- plot_df %>%
  mutate(class = factor(class, levels = c("rainfall", "ROS", "snowmelt"))) %>%
  arrange(class, -prop) %>%
  distinct(site_no)

plot_df <- site_props %>%

type_colors <- c(

p_type_heat <- ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = site_no, y = prop, fill = class)) +

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "05c_adaptive_site_composition_by_class.png"),

p_type_heat
```

#### Within-site rain_frac distributions

The empirical CDFs below show the distribution of `rain_frac` at a sample of sites
spanning the process-dominance spectrum, overlaid with the population-level quartile
cut lines. At most sites the CDF is nearly flat between the two right-hand dashed
lines — the Q3 interval — confirming that the within-site distributions are strongly
bimodal, with mass concentrated near 0 and near 1 and very few peaks in the
intermediate range that Q3 occupies globally.

```{r quartile-ecdf, fig.width = 7.0, fig.height = 6.0}
# Select a representative sample of sites spanning median rain_frac
n_sites_show <- 16

sample_sites <- quart %>%
  filter(data_sufficient, !is.na(rain_frac)) %>%
  group_by(site_no) %>%
  summarise(median_rf = median(rain_frac), n_peaks = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(n_peaks >= 10) %>%
  mutate(rank = ntile(median_rf, n_sites_show)) %>%
  group_by(rank) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(median_rf)

ecdf_df <- quart %>%
  filter(data_sufficient, !is.na(rain_frac),
         site_no %in% sample_sites$site_no) %>%
  left_join(sample_sites %>% select(site_no, median_rf), by = "site_no") %>%
  mutate(site_label = sprintf("%s\n(med=%.2f)", site_no, median_rf),
         site_label = reorder(site_label, median_rf))

# Retrieve quartile breaks stored as attribute
q_breaks <- attr(quart, "quartile_breaks")

p_ecdf <- ggplot(ecdf_df, aes(x = rain_frac)) +
  stat_ecdf(linewidth = 0.7, color = "grey30") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = q_breaks[2:4], linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~site_label, ncol = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "rain_frac", limits = c(0, 1),
                     breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Cumulative proportion", breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Within-site empirical CDFs of rain_frac",
    subtitle = "Dashed lines = population-level quartile boundaries. Sites ordered by median rain_frac."
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 7),
        panel.spacing = unit(0.4, "lines"))

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "05c_quartile_ecdf_within_site.png"),
       p_ecdf, width = 7, height = 6, dpi = 150)
p_ecdf
```

The within-site bimodality of `rain_frac` is not an artifact of pooling heterogeneous
sites — it is a consistent feature of individual Colorado gauges. Most sites see
floods that are either predominantly melt-driven or predominantly rainfall-driven,
with very few events in the intermediate range. The population-level quartile
construction masks this by drawing Q2 and Q3 from sparse contributions spread
across many sites, but no individual site contributes enough peaks to the intermediate
range to support a per-site GPD fit.

The natural remedy would be per-site quantile boundaries, which would guarantee
equal counts per quartile at every site. However this would mean Q1 at a
melt-dominated site and Q1 at a rainfall-dominated site correspond to very different
values of `rain_frac`, stripping the quartile labels of cross-site process-physical
meaning. Since the goal of the quartile FFA is to ask whether process dominance
predicts upper-tail flood behaviour across sites — not just within them — population-level
boundaries are the appropriate choice. Q3 should instead be treated as unrecoverable
at the per-site level with the current design, and the quartile scheme acknowledged as
effectively a three-category split in practice: melt-dominated (Q1), transitional
(Q2), and rainfall-dominated (Q4).
